players.product: AI-ready colocation and hyperscale data centres (including high-density liquid-to-chip capacity) in Sydney, Melbourne, other Australian metros and Kuala Lumpur for cloud, AI, hyperscaler and neocloud deployments

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Craig Scroggie (FY26 results call): the large majority of the half a gigawatt contracted in FY26 is with AA-rated or better counterparties; NEXTDC has some neocloud customers in addition to traditional hyperscalers, and those neocloud customers are backstopped in contract by NVIDIA for a decade or more; hyperscale contracts run a minimum of 10 to 15 years with options of up to 35 years; all AI deployments in Australia today are for inferencing, not training. On the 73 megawatts announced at the end of July he called it 'that Nvidia deal', with NVIDIA as a partner: it is under construction, will activate quickly but back-ended within FY27, largely all at one time.
quarterly_data.figure: 73 megawatts back-ended in FY27; contracts 10 to 15 years with up to 35-year options
quarterly_data.counterparty_role: partner and contractual backstop of NEXTDC's neocloud customers

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Craig Scroggie (FY26 results call): customers have contracted 740 megawatts against 288 built and less than a quarter of contracted capacity is billing; 95% of capacity is contracted across key cloud and AI customers; this year NEXTDC locked its first gigawatt-scale reference architecture, and build-to-suit hyperscale campuses for a 1-gigawatt NVIDIA DSX reference architecture will be single-story buildings; with offsite containerization and a manufacturing-style method he expects to go from ground to a fully operating facility in about nine months versus about 18 months historically; larger sites such as S7 (650 megawatts) and M5 (1,200 megawatts) offer upside to the minimum yield on cost assumed for the 365-megawatt S4 site. He said scale lets NEXTDC manage long-lead constraints such as securing hundreds of generators, and that it has the power certainty needed for the capacity contracted in FY26.
quarterly_data.figure: about nine months ground to operation vs about 18 months; S7 650 megawatts; M5 1,200 megawatts

quarterly_data.signal: FY27 delivery (FY26 results call): CEO Craig Scroggie said 100% of what is required to deliver the FY27 numbers is already locked in, with no new development approvals or power needed; 537 megawatts of built capacity is in progress and a further 130 megawatts in plan; S4's first 250 megawatts is under construction, M4 early works have started with 10 megawatts in progress, S5 is expected to start construction in FY27, KL1 has a further 15 megawatts in progress and 15 in plan, and Tokyo 1 excavation has begun; S5 and S7 await State Significant Development approvals; NEXTDC intends to contract the remaining 115 megawatts of S4 before moving it into a joint-venture structure. Facility costs rose AUD 11.3 million (17%) and corporate costs AUD 11.1 million (17%) ahead of over 400 megawatts of build capacity growth expected across FY 2027 and 2028; available liquidity is AUD 8.7 billion.
quarterly_data.figure: 537 megawatts in progress; 130 megawatts in plan; 115 megawatts of S4 to sell; liquidity AUD 8.7 billion

quarterly_data.signal: CEO Craig Scroggie, management view (FY26 results call): pipeline options and reservations are at a level never seen before and 'demand really is insatiable' across hyperscalers, neoclouds and model builders; demand is shifting toward inference, which must sit close to enterprise and government data, favouring NEXTDC's metro presence; proposed New South Wales and federal energy reforms do not affect the operating portfolio or the 565-megawatt forward order book, while customers remain responsible for procuring the electricity itself.
